needs.title: Crosswalks and stop positions

source_cards.front: Where do you stop on red and when may you turn right
source_cards.back: On red, stop behind the crosswalk or stop line until green, then turn right when the way is clear of cars and pedestrians unless a sign bans it.

source_cards.front: What do the stop sign and the yield sign each look like and order
source_cards.back: An eight-sided red stop sign with white letters orders a stop behind the line or crosswalk plus a yield to crossing traffic and walkers in every direction, and a red-and-white downward triangle yield sign orders slowing until right-of-way traffic passes.

source_cards.front: Where do you halt at a crosswalk, whom do you yield to, and what if no crossing shows
source_cards.back: Crosswalks frame legal pedestrian crossings, so halt behind the stop line, crosswalk, or sign and yield to anyone entering or inside, stay wary since many crossings lack paint, stop ahead of the intersection when no crossing shows, and honor a stop line before the crosswalk first.

needs.title: Intersections and right-of-way

source_cards.front: What do right-of-way rules decide and does anyone own the right of way
source_cards.back: Right-of-way rules set who yields first and the order for entering and crossing intersections, yet nobody ever owns the right of way automatically, so every approach demands a fresh read of the scene.

source_cards.front: Who do you yield to at an intersection, on a left turn, and at a simultaneous four-way stop
source_cards.back: Yield to the driver who arrived first, to opposing traffic including right-turning vehicles when you turn left, and to the driver on your right when both of you reach a four-way stop at once.

source_cards.front: Who wins at an intersection by arrival and at a simultaneous four-way stop
source_cards.back: First arrival wins the intersection, while a simultaneous four-way stop gives the nod to the driver on your right.

source_cards.front: What do the stop sign and the yield sign each look like and order
source_cards.back: An eight-sided red stop sign with white letters orders a stop behind the line or crosswalk plus a yield to crossing traffic and walkers in every direction, and a red-and-white downward triangle yield sign orders slowing until right-of-way traffic passes.

source_cards.front: How does a stop sign differ from a yield sign
source_cards.back: The eight-sided red stop sign orders a complete halt, while the downward red-and-white triangle only orders slowing for right-of-way traffic.

source_cards.back: Stacked signals read red over yellow over green from the top, while horizontal city signals read red left, yellow center, and green right, with lone single-color lights posted at some spots.

source_cards.front: Where do you stop on red and when may you turn right

source_cards.front: What do orange work-zone signs mark and what must you obey there

needs.title: Traffic and pedestrian signals

source_cards.front: What does a green light allow and what does a left on green still wait for
source_cards.back: A green light lets you go straight or turn after yielding to everyone lawfully in the intersection, and a left on green still waits for opposing through traffic.

source_cards.front: What do steady green, flashing yellow, upward green, and red arrows each mean
source_cards.back: A steady green arrow sends you that way from the proper lane, a flashing yellow arrow urges a careful proceed, an upward green arrow means straight ahead, and a red arrow bans that turn until green, always obeying the head above your lane.

source_cards.front: How does a steady green arrow differ from a flashing yellow arrow
source_cards.back: A steady green arrow grants the turn from the proper lane, while a flashing yellow arrow only permits a careful proceed.

needs.title: Other traffic signs

source_cards.front: What does a yellow railroad warning sign mean and when must you stop at a crossbuck
source_cards.back: The round yellow railroad warning sign means tracks are ahead: reduce speed, look and listen, and prepare to stop for a train. At the white crossbuck, an approaching train or rail vehicle requires stopping behind the line or before the crossing until it is clear.

source_cards.front: What do regulatory signs look like and what does a red ring and slash mean
source_cards.back: Regulatory signs speak the law in white squares, rectangles, or special shapes with black, red, or green markings, covering direction, lanes, turns, speed, and parking, with a red ring and slash banning the pictured act, while black-and-white speed boards cap legal speed for ideal conditions.

source_cards.front: What do shared center lane, one-way, wrong-way, and do-not-enter signs each mean
source_cards.back: A shared center lane serves left turns from either side only and never through traffic or passing, one-way signs permit travel in the arrow's direction alone, wrong-way signs warn you are headed against traffic at ramps and one-way starts, and do-not-enter signs bar entry at those same spots.

source_cards.front: What colors are guide signs and where do they point
source_cards.back: Guide signs in green, brown, or blue squares and rectangles point to crossing roads, towns, sights, hospitals, fuel, food, and lodging.

source_cards.front: How does advance railroad warning differ from the crossbuck stop condition
source_cards.back: A round yellow railroad sign gives advance warning of tracks; at the white crossbuck, stop behind the line or before the crossing when a train or rail vehicle approaches, and wait for a clear crossing.

source_cards.front: What color and shape are warning signs and when is fluorescent yellow used
source_cards.back: Warning signs flag possible danger ahead in black on yellow diamonds, urging slower speed and stop readiness, with fluorescent yellow reserved for school zones, school crossings, and pedestrian crossings.

needs.title: Freeway entry and exit

source_cards.front: How do you join a freeway and who has the right of way
source_cards.back: Join freeways via the acceleration lane at traffic speed through a chosen gap with a cancelled signal, yielding to traffic already there.

source_cards.front: How do you plan and execute a freeway exit
source_cards.back: Choose the lane nearest your exit well ahead of time and keep your current speed on the main roadway. Signal before moving into the deceleration lane, then slow down and check that lane’s posted speed.

source_cards.front: How do freeway entries and exits differ in speed handling
source_cards.back: Highway entries speed up in the acceleration lane and yield to existing flow, while exits hold speed and then slow in the deceleration lane.

source_cards.front: What are the lane roles on multi-lane and two-lane roads and what left-lane habit is illegal
source_cards.back: Three-or-more lanes give middles to through traffic, the left to passers and left-turners, and the right to slower, entering, and right-turning drivers, while two-lane roads flow smoothest right with the left saved for passing, and camping the left lane of a limited-access highway breaks the law.

source_cards.front: On which side do you pass, when may you pass right, and when may you leave the roadway
source_cards.back: Pass on the left as a rule with the left-most lane reserved for it, pass right only when truly safe since right-side cars hide and surprise, and never leave the roadway unless the passed car fully stops and the move stays safe.

source_cards.back: Manage speed for roads and traffic, keep a real following gap, obey posted limits, and glance at the speedometer about once a minute.

source_cards.front: What does total stopping distance span and how long is perception time
source_cards.back: Total stopping distance spans realization to rest under ideal conditions, grows with speed, and starts with perception time averaging three quarters second to one second in alert drivers.

source_cards.front: How long is reaction time and how far is braking distance from fifty
source_cards.back: Reaction time from gas to brake averages three quarters second to one second, and braking distance from pedal to rest runs about one hundred fifty-eight feet from fifty miles per hour on dry pavement with sound brakes.

source_cards.front: How does total stopping distance differ from perception time
source_cards.back: Total stopping distance spans realization to rest, while perception time covers only the recognition slice.

source_cards.back: Reaction time moves the foot in three quarters second to one second, while braking distance then spends about one hundred fifty-eight feet from fifty miles per hour

source_cards.front: What does a space cushion buy and where do you keep it
source_cards.back: A space cushion in every direction buys reaction time, so guard open room around your car at all times.

source_cards.front: What is hydroplaning and how do you avoid it
source_cards.back: Hydroplaning floats steering tires onto pooled water like skis with zero road contact, so slow down on wet roads, keep tires firm and treaded, and never drive through large standing water but reroute instead.

needs.title: Skid and traction recovery

source_cards.front: What causes skids and what makes them worse
source_cards.back: Skids strike from excess speed, panic stops, or lost grip and leave little control, while panicking, brake-stomping, and overcorrecting only deepen the skid toward a fatal crash.

source_cards.front: How do you recover from a sideways skid
source_cards.back: In a sideways skid, steer toward the sliding rear to realign the nose, then unwind promptly as the car straightens to block a counter-skid.

source_cards.front: How long do you keep correcting and which control matters most in a skid
source_cards.back: Keep seesawing the wheel until the skid fully releases, since the steering wheel outranks every other skid control.

source_cards.front: What is the sequence for a sideways skid
source_cards.back: Sideways skids steer into the sliding rear, then unwind fast to block the counter-skid.

source_cards.front: What do you do when the brakes fail while rolling
source_cards.back: Brakeless while rolling, drag the parking brake slowly against rear-wheel lockup and skid, poised to release if the tail steps out.

needs.title: Vehicle blind spots

source_cards.front: How much room and following distance do motorcycles get
source_cards.back: Motorcycles share full road rights and duties yet hide easily, so grant a whole lane always, sweep mirrors and blind spots, study fronts and flanks before lefts, distrust sticky signals until the turn proves real, and trail by four seconds or more, longer when wet.

source_cards.front: How common are car-commercial crashes and why do rigs differ from cars
source_cards.back: Over two hundred fifty thousand car-commercial crashes strike yearly yet mostly avoidably, since big rigs dwarf cars in size, blind spots, stopping and rolling distances, and turning girth.

source_cards.front: Where are a truck's side no-zones worst and how do you avoid them
source_cards.back: Side no-zones swallow cars beside tractors and buses, worst on the right from behind the cab down the trailer length, so trade mirror-face sightlines and shun lingering alongside where swerves kill.

source_cards.front: How far behind a truck is its blind zone and what do trucks do on grades
source_cards.back: Rear no-zones blind trucks to two hundred feet behind, so follow loose and mirror-visible with an escape in mind, while grades pin trucks near thirty-five miles per hour in the right lane, which you should vacate near hills and weigh stations.

source_cards.front: What does Kentucky law require for blind walkers and where do you halt
source_cards.back: Kentucky law yields the road to blind walkers with visible white canes or assistance dogs under a two hundred fifty dollars fine, so halt within five feet of the crosswalk short of advance bars to stay audible, and mind silent electrics and hybrids.

source_cards.front: What should you never do around a blind crosser
source_cards.back: Never talk a blind crosser across since they read traffic sound, never wait them out forever, roll when they step back and pocket the cane, never plug the crosswalk and force a traffic detour, and never honk at their confusion and fright.

source_cards.front: Which walkers earn readiness and which command the yield
source_cards.back: Walkers anywhere earn readiness, while crosswalk and intersection walkers command the yield.
